title: A fault-tolerant quantum blockchain deployed on commercial telecommunications network
authors: Yongqiang Du, Chen-Xun Weng, Feng Xie, Ming-Yang Li, Mingxuan Zhang, Xin Hua, Xin An, Xiang Guan, Xin Liu, Zhenrong Zhang, Xi Xiao, Hua-Lei Yin, Kejin Wei
abstract: Popularized by the Bitcoin cryptocurrency, blockchain technology establishes a decentralized digital framework that utilizes cryptographic and consensus protocols to secure data against unauthorized modification. Consequently, blockchain has found broad adoption across diverse fields, including finance, data management, healthcare, and digital asset governance. In the quantum computing era, a paramount objective for blockchain is to preserve its foundational advantages of cryptographic integrity and decentralized fault-tolerant resilience. In principle, quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement protocols offer foundational security guarantees and tolerate up to one-half of malicious nodes for blockchain. However, the practical realization of such a quantum-enhanced blockchain remains a significant and multifaceted challenge. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a fully operational hybrid quantum blockchain architecture built on photonic integrated circuits and deployed over commercially available classical telecommunications infrastructure. The system achieves a fault tolerance of nearly one-half, surpassing the classical limit, while reaching consensus on a timescale of seconds. A deployed food traceability application validates the practicality of the proposed architecture, achieving a throughput of approximately 500 transactions per second. This work establishes a foundation for practical quantum blockchains, enabling secure, scalable, and decentralized information processing in the emerging quantum era.
summary: This paper presents an experimental demonstration of a hybrid quantum blockchain designed for practical use in supply chain management. By deploying protocols like Quantum Byzantine Agreement over commercial fiber optics, the system achieves superior fault tolerance and high throughput. It establishes a viable blueprint for secure, scalable, and decentralized information processing in the emerging quantum era.
main_problem: The core problem is ensuring that blockchain technology maintains its cryptographic integrity and decentralized fault-tolerant resilience when operating in the quantum computing era.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a fully operational hybrid quantum blockchain architecture achieving fault tolerance approaching one-half, surpassing classical limits, with a practical throughput of 500 transactions per second for food traceability.
method: They proposed and experimentally implemented a four-layer hybrid architecture combining Quantum Byzantine Agreement (QBA) protocols with photonic integrated circuits deployed over commercial fiber networks.
model_or_system: The system is built on a five-user network in Nanning, China, utilizing photonic integrated circuits for the quantum physical layer. It integrates classical blockchain frameworks (Hyperledger Fabric) with quantum primitives like BB84 QKD and OTUH-QDS signatures.
key_observables: Fault tolerance approaching one-half; throughput of approximately 500 transactions per second; secure key rates up to 273.49 kbps.
important_parameters: Five nodes (N=5) tolerating two malicious participants (f=2); link loss of 13.2 dB over an average length of 13.1 km.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the feasibility of integrating quantum advantages into existing, commercially available classical telecommunications infrastructure for real-world deployment.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the four-layer architecture workflow; Figure 2 shows the star-like physical network topology in Nanning; Figure 3 details the six stages of the food traceability application flow from input to viewing results.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the quantum blockchain challenge, proposes the layered hybrid architecture (Application $ightarrow$ Quantum Consensus $ightarrow$ Classical Logical $ightarrow$ Quantum Physical), details the implementation using QKD and QBA protocols over a metropolitan fiber network, validates it with an end-to-end food traceability application, and concludes by establishing its foundation for practical quantum data processing.
why_interesting: This work represents a direct engineering demonstration of applying advanced quantum information concepts (QKD, QBA) to solve a complex distributed systems problem (blockchain), which is highly relevant to the physical realization of quantum networks.
